passage:
Monday: Rajni announced that the stock-count feature would go ahead and the reports redesign would wait until next quarter. Simran's team, who wanted the reports, said nothing in the meeting and did not look up.

Thursday: Rajni noticed the team's replies had turned short and a ticket from them sat untouched. She realised the announcement had given the decision without the reasons. She asked Simran for half an hour and, at the tea counter, explained: the stock-count feature was tied to a customer contract, and the redesign had no such date. Simran said it still stung. Rajni asked what would help, and they agreed on a check-in in six weeks and a small fix to the two worst reports.

Following Tuesday: Simran's team sent their ticket again, and Simran asked to join the next planning meeting early.

qa.q: What did Rajni and Simran agree on at the tea counter?
qa.a: They agreed on a check-in in six weeks and a small fix to the two worst reports.

qa.q: What was Rajni worried about when the replies turned short?
qa.a: Rajni worried the team felt shut out and the working relationship would suffer, having realised the announcement gave the decision without the reasons.

qa.q: What could Rajni do next time to avoid the cold reaction?
qa.a: Rajni could talk to the affected team before the announcement, or give the reasons at the same moment as the decision.

qa.q: How did the change of approach look to Simran?
qa.a: Simran received reasons and a follow-up, which probably eased the sting, and asking to join planning early suggests renewed trust.

grounding: Shows a lead noticing a disappointed team's silence, explaining the reasons in person and agreeing a follow-up on their concerns.

subtype: Approach: explaining the decision to those who lost [Revision]
passage: Manoj, you think the decision is finished once you announce it. Let your Nirmala ma'am tell you it isn't. I was twenty-six, leading my first project, and I had to choose between the Chennai team's design and the Pune team's. I chose Chennai's. I sent one email and moved on. For three months, Pune did the minimum. Every review, cold faces. Then I understood. So I took a train to Pune. I sat with them in their small meeting room and told them why: Chennai's design was cheaper to run, not better built. I told them which part of their idea I wanted in the next version, and I gave them a date. The room changed. That team later saved us on a much bigger project. They told me it was because I came.

qa.q: Which team's design did Nirmala choose?
How did Nirmala feel during the three months of cold faces?
qa.a: She likely felt uneasy and puzzled, sensing a problem with the Pune team before she understood why.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Nirmala's story?
qa.a: Taking the train to Pune to explain the reasons in person and agree a follow-up, which kept the relationship alive.

qa.q: How might the Pune team have felt when Nirmala came?
qa.a: They likely felt respected and heard at last, since she explained the choice and promised their idea a place later.

grounding: It shows a lead meeting the disappointed team after a choice, explaining the reasons and agreeing a follow-up, keeping the relationship intact.

subtype: Approach: explaining the decision to those who lost [Revision]
passage:
Hemant's flight to Delhi was at six the next morning, and his bag was already in the car. But the decision had gone out at four: the Hyderabad team's billing design would be built, not the design from Manjula's team in Bengaluru. He had seen Manjula's face on the video call. She had said nothing.
So at seven, instead of going home, he called Manjula and asked if her team could stay for thirty minutes on video. Six tired faces appeared. He explained the reasons plainly: faster to build, fits the old system, not a judgement on their skill. Then he asked what worried them most. 'That our work just disappears,' Manjula said. They agreed that her team's reporting idea would be the first item in next quarter's plan, with a review in January. He left the office at eight, the rain just starting.

qa.q: What was Manjula worried about most?
qa.a: Manjula was worried and hurt that her team's work would simply disappear.

qa.q: What else could Hemant do after landing in Delhi?
qa.a: He could send a short written summary of the reasons and the January review, so the promise is on record.

qa.q: How might Manjula's team see Hemant staying late before a flight?
qa.a: They may feel respected, seeing that the lead cared enough to explain face to face instead of by email.

grounding: It shows a lead meeting the disappointed team after a decision, explaining the reasons and agreeing a follow-up for their concerns.
